promptText: Why can't an LLM-backed feature be evaluated the same way a JUnit test evaluates a normal Java method?
options: JUnit tests cannot be run in a CI/CD pipeline, but LLM evaluations can

A JUnit assertion checks deterministic, exact-match behavior; an LLM's output is probabilistic, so the same input can produce different, sometimes equally valid or subtly wrong outputs across runs, making exact-match assertions brittle and requiring statistical evaluation instead
LLM outputs are always identical across runs, making testing trivial and unnecessary
JUnit only supports integer return types, which LLM APIs never produce
explanation: Because output is probabilistic, evaluation needs statistical sampling and rubric-based or LLM-as-judge scoring with a confidence interval, rather than a single pass/fail exact-match assertion.

promptText: What is LLM-as-judge, and why did the field adopt it instead of having humans grade every output?
options: It replaces the production model entirely with a rules-based scoring engine

It uses a strong model to grade another model's output against a rubric, because human grading does not scale to production evaluation volumes or CI/CD release cadences; humans still calibrate the judge and review disagreements
It is a benchmark like MMLU used only to compare foundation models before purchase
It requires no rubric at all, since the judge model infers correctness from training data alone
explanation: LLM-as-judge makes evaluating open-ended tasks affordable at scale by concentrating expensive human review on calibration and disagreement cases rather than grading every single output.

promptText: What question does task-level (end-to-end) evaluation answer, as distinct from component-level and system-level evaluation?
options: Is the deployed product achieving its business goal over real traffic and time?
Given a full user request, is the final answer correct, helpful, and safe?
Is CPU and memory usage within acceptable bounds?
Is this one isolated piece, like the retriever, doing its narrow job correctly?
explanation: Component-level checks isolated pieces (like retrieval recall@k), task-level checks the full end-to-end response quality (often via LLM-as-judge), and system-level checks the business outcome over real production traffic — the three layers answer different questions and can diverge from one another.

promptText: What does a wide confidence interval around a measured pass rate practically tell an engineer?
options: The evaluation pipeline has a software bug that must be fixed before shipping
The true underlying pass rate could plausibly be quite different from the single measured point estimate, so small swings between runs may just be sampling noise rather than a real change
The judge model used an incorrect API key
The sample size was too large and should be reduced
explanation: With a small sample, a 3-point swing in pass rate between runs is often well within noise; a tight confidence interval — achieved with a larger sample — is needed before treating a measured change as real.

promptText: Why does a mature evaluation rubric score groundedness, correctness, and helpfulness as separate dimensions instead of one combined 'quality score'?
options: Because rubric frameworks technically forbid combining more than one criterion

Because these three properties fail independently and point to different fixes — a groundedness failure points at retrieval/citation logic, a correctness failure at knowledge base freshness, and a helpfulness failure at prompt design — so collapsing them destroys diagnostic value
Because LLM-as-judge models can only output one score per API call
Because groundedness and correctness are mathematically identical and only helpfulness differs
explanation: An answer can be grounded but wrong (if the source material itself was wrong), or correct but unhelpful; scoring them separately tells you exactly where in the pipeline to look when a dimension regresses.

promptText: What is the core limitation of BLEU/ROUGE-style overlap metrics for evaluating open-ended generative tasks?
options: They can only be computed on multiple-choice questions, never on free text
They require a live internet connection to a model provider to compute

They measure surface-level n-gram similarity to a reference answer, not meaning or correctness — a summary with the right meaning in different words scores poorly, while one that copies phrasing but subtly reverses meaning can score well
They only work for code generation tasks, not natural language
explanation: Overlap metrics were a genuine advance over nothing, letting researchers iterate without paying humans to grade every output, but the automated-vs-shallow trade-off they introduced is exactly why enterprise LLM evaluation later moved toward LLM-as-judge for open-ended tasks.

promptText: Why should an LLM-as-judge model be periodically calibrated against human labels using a metric like Cohen's kappa, rather than trusted indefinitely once validated?
options: Cohen's kappa is required by law for any AI evaluation system

Judge models are themselves models that can change behavior across provider updates or drift over time, so if judge-human agreement drops below an agreed threshold, the judge prompt or model must be revised before its verdicts are trusted again
Calibration is only needed once, at the very first deployment, and never again afterward
Cohen's kappa measures token cost, not agreement, so it is unrelated to judge reliability
explanation: Judge calibration is a mathematical precondition for the rest of the evaluation pipeline meaning anything — a judge with poor agreement against human labels adds noise that can swamp the very effect you are trying to measure.

promptText: A prompt change raises the pass rate from 91% to 94% on a 25-case evaluation set. Should this be treated as a confirmed improvement?
options: Yes, any measured increase should be shipped immediately regardless of sample size

No — with only 25 samples, the confidence interval around a 91-94% pass rate is wide enough that a 3-point swing is very plausibly noise rather than a real gain; a larger, segmented run is needed before concluding the change helped
Yes, because LLM-as-judge scores are always exact and require no statistical interpretation
No, because pass rates can never be compared across two different prompt versions
explanation: Five samples or twenty-five samples cannot reliably distinguish a real improvement from sampling variance; sizing an evaluation set to the effect size you care about detecting is a core discipline of this chapter.

promptText: Why should evaluation results be sliced by segment (language, customer tier, query category) rather than only reviewed as a single aggregate pass rate?
options: Segmentation is only useful for billing purposes, not quality assessment
An aggregate pass rate can hide a specific segment failing badly while being averaged out by segments performing well, a pattern analogous to Simpson's paradox
Segmented results always produce a higher headline number than aggregate results
Slicing by segment eliminates the need for confidence intervals entirely
explanation: A shrinking but important segment can quietly regress while the overall number holds steady or even improves, so segment-level dashboards are necessary to catch what a single headline metric would mask.

promptText: What is the Goodhart's Law risk specific to an LLM evaluation program, and how is it typically guarded against?
options: The risk that engineers start prompt-tuning specifically to make the judge happy rather than to better serve users, causing the metric and the real goal to diverge; it is guarded against by periodically checking judge scores against system-level (business) metrics
The risk that the judge model runs out of context window space during scoring
The risk that evaluation datasets become too large to store, guarded against by deleting old cases
The risk that human reviewers disagree with each other, guarded against by using only automated checks
explanation: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure; if judge scores climb while real user outcomes stay flat or worsen, that is a sign the judge itself has drifted from what actually matters.

promptText: Why must an evaluation harness invoke the exact same ChatClient/Advisor chain that production uses, rather than a simplified or mocked call path?
options: Spring AI technically forbids calling the same ChatClient bean twice
Evaluating a code path that differs even slightly from production (a different Advisor chain, different retrieval configuration) produces numbers that do not transfer to real user-facing behavior
A simplified path always runs faster, so it is preferred whenever speed matters more than accuracy
Mocked call paths are required to avoid violating a model provider's terms of service
explanation: The whole point of the evaluation number is that it predicts real behavior; if guardrails, retrieval, or memory advisors differ between the evaluated path and production, the measured score no longer reflects what a user actually experiences.

promptText: Why do mature evaluation pipelines run each test case multiple times (commonly 3-5 repetitions) at a controlled sampling temperature rather than once?
options: Repetitions are required by most model providers' rate-limit policies

Because the same input can produce different outputs across runs due to non-determinism, so a single run's pass/fail is treated as one noisy sample rather than ground truth, and the pass rate across repetitions becomes the actual signal
Running a case multiple times reduces the total token cost of the evaluation
Repetitions are only needed for deterministic checks, never for LLM-as-judge scoring
explanation: Non-determinism has to be actively managed: a single run could pass or fail somewhat by chance, so aggregating pass rate across repetitions gives a more reliable estimate of the system's actual behavior on that case.

promptText: A product leader wants to switch production from an expensive frontier model to a cheaper one, and the offline evaluation suite shows the aggregate pass rate holding steady. What additional evidence should make a staff engineer say no to the switch despite the steady aggregate?
options: Nothing further is needed — a steady aggregate pass rate is sufficient proof the switch is safe to fully roll out

A regression in any single rubric dimension (e.g., groundedness) beyond its confidence interval, a high-value or high-risk segment regressing even while the aggregate holds, or a canary rollout showing real user outcomes worsening despite clean offline numbers
The switch should always be blocked regardless of evaluation results, since cost changes are never worth a quality risk
Only the token cost comparison matters; quality dimensions are irrelevant once cost is confirmed lower
explanation: A cheaper model might match on tone but regress specifically on groundedness or numerical correctness, or degrade disproportionately on a rare but high-value segment the aggregate averages away — offline evaluation is necessary but not sufficient, which is why a staged canary is required regardless of how clean the offline numbers look.

promptText: Why does a mature, heavily-optimized production system need an order of magnitude more evaluation cases than an early prototype to responsibly measure progress?
options: Mature systems are legally required to test more cases under most AI governance frameworks

As easy gains are captured over time, the marginal improvements worth measuring get smaller, and because confidence interval width shrinks roughly with 1/√n, detecting a smaller true effect reliably requires a proportionally much larger sample size
Mature systems always have more bugs than prototypes, requiring more test coverage
Larger evaluation sets are needed only because mature systems have more code, not because of any statistical reason
explanation: A prototype needs only enough cases to catch gross regressions with large effect sizes; a mature system's remaining improvements are often just 1-2 points, and quadrupling sample size only roughly halves the noise band, so meaningfully tighter confidence intervals require substantially more cases.

promptText: Why is using the exact model currently being improved as its own uncalibrated judge a methodological trap, rather than just a convenience?
options: It is purely a cost problem with no methodological consequence, since the same model call is simply reused

A judge sharing the system-under-test's own blind spots or stylistic preferences will systematically overrate outputs that share those biases, and without independent calibration against human labels this drift toward self-flattering scores can compound with Goodhart's Law as engineers optimize toward the judge's approval rather than real user value
Uncalibrated self-judging is only a problem for classification tasks, never for open-ended generation
Model providers technically prohibit a model from ever judging its own output
explanation: Two failure modes compound: shared blind spots make the judge an unreliable arbiter of the very system it evaluates, and without calibration against independent human labels, engineers can inadvertently optimize toward pleasing the judge rather than improving real outcomes — exactly the Goodhart's Law dynamic the chapter warns against.
